newsitem.title: UK: BritGas may seek "showdown" on contracts - report.
newsitem.headline: BritGas may seek "showdown" on contracts - report.

text.p: The liabilities faced by British Gas over long-term purchase contracts may encourage it to seek a "showdown" with producers, energy analysts said in a report on Thursday.
"The possibility cannot be ruled out that British Gas seek to bring the issue to a head through some form of show-down," the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies (OIES) report said.
"Under almost all conceivable scenarios, the market is set to become increasingly fractious, non-cooperative and possibly litigious," it continued.
The OIES said the chance of voluntary contracts renegotiation involving the effective transfer of funds from gas producers to British Gas Energy is slight, as long as the latter appears solvent.
But confrontation was not seen the most likely outcome.

"The most likely outcome is one of drift, in which all parties hope that the market trends will alleviate the current tensions and, if not, wait for them to worsen so that minds are concentrated," the OIES report said.

In the first half of 1995, the development of the deregulated gas market in Britain led to a halving of spot gas prices. This left companies buying gas under long-term contracts at fixed prices - especially British Gas - facing large potential losses.
The OIES report concluded that the gas market in Britain will remain oversupplied until the Interconnector pipeline allowing exports to Belgium and the rest of Europe comes onstream in late 1998.
But this is unlikely to solve the contract problem, it adds, saying U.K. contract prices are likely to remain above prices elsewhere in Europe.

The report saw little chance for a political solution, pointing out that the difference between spot and contract gas prices has given a major boost to the government's policy of introducing competition.
"To redress the balance between gas costs would work against this objective", it said.
While the difference between spot and contract prices remains, the higher prices will be passed on to residential users, the OIES said.
"While the market open to competition benefits from cheaper gas, the monopoly residential market is likely to shoulder part of the cost of old contracts", it added.
